reason: The provided sources contain extensive multi-cited details about the historic 1833 Leonid storm and its role in founding meteor science.
story: On the night of November 12-13, 1833, the night sky over North America exploded into a fiery blizzard. Up to 240,000 meteors fell over nine hours, terrifying onlookers who feared the end of the world. At the time, mainstream scientists believed shooting stars were atmospheric phenomena like lightning. But Yale professor Denison Olmsted noticed something revolutionary: every meteor appeared to radiate from a single stationary point in the constellation Leo. By collecting accounts from across the continent, Olmsted proved that meteors originate from a cloud of cosmic debris in outer space. Astronomers later connected the Leonids to comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves behind dense dust trails every 33 years. What began as an apocalyptic nightmare transformed human understanding of space, establishing the modern science of meteors.
angle: The 1833 Leonid meteor storm was so intense—peaking at over 100,000 meteors per hour—that it proved meteors come from outer space rather than Earth's atmosphere, birthing meteor science.

claims.claim: The Leonid meteor shower occurs annually in mid-November.
The Leonids originate from debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle.
Comet Tempel-Tuttle orbits the Sun approximately once every 33 years.
Leonid meteoroids impact Earth's atmosphere at speeds of about 45 miles per second (70 kilometers per second).
The shower gets its name because its meteors appear to radiate from the constellation Leo.
On the night of November 12 to 13, 1833, a massive meteor storm struck North America.
Peak estimates for the 1833 meteor storm ranged between 100,000 and 240,000 meteors per hour.
Before the 1833 event, meteors were widely thought to be atmospheric weather phenomena rather than celestial objects.
Yale professor Denison Olmsted analyzed the 1833 storm and determined that the meteors originated from a cloud of particles in outer space.
Explorer Alexander von Humboldt documented a major Leonid meteor display over Venezuela in 1799.
Historic accounts of Leonid meteor storms date back to 902 AD, when Chinese and Arab observers described stars falling like rain.
In 1966, another massive Leonid storm produced peak rates of up to 40 meteors per second over the western United States.
The anticipated 1899 Leonid storm failed to appear because Jupiter's gravitational pull shifted the meteoroid stream.
Comet Tempel-Tuttle was lost to observers for nearly a century before being rediscovered in 1965.
In Boston, eyewitnesses of the 1833 storm estimated meteor frequency to be about half that of falling flakes in an average snowstorm.
Gravitational interactions with Jupiter make historic-scale Leonid storms unlikely for several decades.

disputed: Exact peak hourly meteor count for the 1833 storm varies between sources (50,000 to 240,000 meteors per hour); a script should state 'an estimated 100,000 to over 200,000 meteors per hour'.
Whether an earlier storm occurred in Cumana in 1766 is noted as a rumour; script should leave out or attribute as 'according to rumor'.
The 1933 absence was blamed by some on Uranus perturbations or bad weather; script should focus on the confirmed Jupiter perturbations.
